desk.headline: HEPS up 50.5% to 850.3c on strong US fishmeal and hake despite a Lucky Star fish shortage; revenue down 4.2% to R9.6bn; total dividend 430c; shortage expected to last into 2027

other.label: Daybrook (US fishmeal and oil) operating profit

results: HEPS jumped 50.5% to 850.3c even though revenue fell 4.2% to R9.6bn; operating profit rose 20.8% to R1.51bn.
Daybrook in the US was the star, lifting operating profit 56.2% to R839m as fishmeal sales rose 27%; hake-led wild caught seafood grew profit 44.1% to R320m.
Lucky Star sold 8% fewer cartons (8.7m) as a global shortage of frozen fish for canning hit, and local cannery output fell 64%, yet its profit rose 13.2% to R530m.
The African fishmeal business swung to a R175m loss after industrial fish landings fell 70%.
Cash from operations rose 79% and net debt nearly halved to R1.37bn; the total dividend rose to 430c from 285c.

guidance.summary: Oceana gives no earnings targets. It expects low stock and tight frozen pilchard supply to limit Lucky Star volumes in 2027, with customers kept on allocation, while Daybrook should have a strong first half thanks to high opening stock and pre-agreed fish oil prices.

points: CEO Neville Brink said the canned fish shortage will continue into the new financial year, with customers kept on allocations while frozen fish is sourced abroad.
He said about 80% of what Oceana cans comes from outside South Africa, so the global shortage hit production hard.
Lucky Star prices rose in November; Brink said the aim is to keep it affordable and cut costs elsewhere, including fixed costs at the West Coast canneries.
He said newer lines such as canned meat, noodles and spices are growing but will take time to match canned fish.
call.source: Business Day (27 Nov 2026) and EWN (26 Nov 2026) coverage of the results
